issues.issue: "Combos and 5/3 sheets will be 'kicked off' in variables of five" uses trade shorthand that the Agreement nowhere defines, and "The Sunday completes will be continued to kick off as heretofore" points to an unrecorded practice. Neither obligation is ascertainable from the instrument.

The parties agree only to "observe the new conveyor system to determine manpower requirements," without saying who decides, by what standard, or what happens if they disagree. The manning consequence of the installation is left open.

These relief times (20 minutes per trailer, 15 per suburban or mail bag truck) duplicate the relief periods promised in the Carlstadt minutes under 22-A, which state them as a continuation of what "the office will continue to give." Whether the same relief is owed once or under two separate undertakings is unclear.

Relief disputes "will be brought to Theodore Kheel for decision," naming an individual rather than an office, while Section 16 routes disputes over interpretation and application of the Agreement to the Joint Standing Committee and Appeals Board. Nothing provides for Mr. Kheel's unavailability or for the overlap with Section 16.

The decisions "relate to the future; they are prospective," and 2-E.2 continues to apply to existing runs "until they are in force" — with no statement of when or how they come into force. The trigger for the whole interpretive memorandum is missing.

Section 2-E.2 applies fully "except as to such modifications as are described in this letter," though the document is headed as a memorandum of committee decisions and no letter is identified. Which writing carries the modifications is left uncertain.

The Times "will begin to apply the principle" that common-carrier over-the-road trucking will be done by covered employees, a duty of commencement with no completion date or pace. The exceptions turn on runs "now being done by common carrier," again fixed to no date.

Disagreement over the location of a transfer point is to be "considered a dispute under Section 16," whereas 2-E.2(e) provides that such a dispute "shall be presented to the Impartial Chairman for final and binding decision." Two different fora are given the same question.

Drivers who work 45 hours without a fifth shift receive "benefit credits as if they worked the fifth shift (vacation, sick days, pension and welfare, etc.)," which cannot be squared with 13-H.1 and 13-I.1 measuring contributions by shifts actually worked up to five per payroll week. Whether a contribution is owed for a shift not worked is unresolved.

The obligations are keyed to "By January 1, 1974" and to runs "presently delivered," dates and facts long superseded when this 1981-84 book was executed, and performance is excused if "legal action cannot resolve the problem." What survives of the paragraph, and who judges the legal impossibility, is unstated.

Run time is one hour per 27 miles "in a run direct from The Times to a single destination," and for multi-destination runs the clause says only that "allowance will be made." The allowance is neither quantified nor assigned to anyone to fix.

The opening words are mutilated — "Paragraph (h) will be construed clude this stipulation" — dropping the operative "to include." The manner in which paragraph (h) is qualified must be supplied by the reader.

The paragraph announces that as baggage work "drops off, the assignments of these men will be changed as follows" without stating any measure or trigger for the reduction in work. The changes in paragraphs 2 and 3 are made to depend on an event nobody is given power to declare.

The employee may decline the increase only by submitting a form "by the deadline date clearly stated on the form," a date the Agreement neither fixes nor constrains. The employee's right depends entirely on a term supplied unilaterally later.

The loading schedule reads "bundle weight of 87 to 46 pounds, five high," a range that is impossible as printed (37 is plainly meant) and that would in any event exceed the 46-pound maximum set by 3-A.1. The Saturday-night exception for "a reasonable number of bundles" is likewise unmeasured.

The reservation preserves The Times' right to seek damages "with respect to any future incident," a category left entirely undefined and untethered to any breach of this Agreement. Nothing limits it to conduct of the kind that produced the vacated judgment.

Monthly installments of $1,250 on a principal of $177,844 would run for well over a decade, while the contemporaneous News letter promises that "when the six payments referred to in the Memorandum have been made ... The News will not, under any circumstances, require additional payments." The installment schedule and the six-payment discharge cannot both be given effect.

The Union gets the benefit of "more favorable terms or treatment" accorded any other labor organization on an arbitration award or judicial decree, with no measure of comparison and no procedure for determining favorability. The clause then says the agreement "will be amended accordingly" without saying by whom.

Acceleration is triggered if the Union violates "the provisions against strikes and disruptions of orderly relationships with the New York News," a description that matches 16-N only in part and adds an undefined category of disruption. What conduct accelerates the balance is unclear.

Thirty days' notice is required before "any major change in its operations which has an impact on a significant number of its NMDU employees," with neither "major" nor "significant number" defined and only one illustrative example given. The notice duty also stands beside 16-M.3, which requires prior consent rather than notice for a change in condition.

This memorandum leaves the meaning of Section 16-M to a written arbitral decision to be rendered later, incorporating "the three points concerning changed conditions" from a 1971 award in a different union's arbitration. The operative content of 16-M.3 is thus supplied by documents outside the Agreement.

"Every memorandum, letter agreement or side agreement shall be continued through the term of this agreement and deemed updated" cannot be squared with the reprinted memoranda that state their own expiry (21-B.4 ending March 30, 1975; 21-G.3 expiring in three years) or with 21-D.VIII's supersession of all other Newspoint agreements. What "deemed updated" does to dated and terminated side agreements is unaddressed.

The utility man may be assigned to jobs "including but not limited to" three examples, yet the same paragraph makes clearing log jams work that "may only be performed by the utility man." The open-ended assignment power and the exclusive reservation pull in opposite directions.

The floor-hire floor of eighty-one excludes "the 'Alco Men' or people performing functions other than regular floor work on the daily product," a class defined by an undefined trade label. "Normal reduction in press utilization" is likewise unmeasured.

Regular situation holders are "guaranteed against a change in their present starting times," while 5-J expressly permits the Publisher to change a regular situation holder's reporting time on four days' notice. The guarantee and the reserved right cover the same men.
The route "shall be filed by in-shop bidding," plainly a mistranscription of "filled," and no bidding procedure is identified. Section 4-B's posting and bidding rules are not referred to.

The Publishers commit to a posting practice "including, but not limited to, starting times and days off and job functions," then add that "these practices do not limit either party's rights under the collective bargaining agreement." The disclaimer may negate the obligation the letter creates.

The parity promise on pension, welfare and insurance benefits is defeated where improvements are "granted in exchange for productivity improvements (as determined to the Union's reasonable satisfaction) or are diverted from the negotiated pattern package," two exceptions with no defined content and one committed to the Union's own satisfaction. Whether an increase is caught by the promise is unascertainable.

The existing arbitrators remain on the list until a new list is selected "in the manner provided by the parties' Agreement," while 16-E.2 requires selection "immediately after the execution of this Agreement" and 16-E.3 fixes annual striking dates. The letter holds open a list the Agreement directs to be constituted at once.

The Publisher agrees to amend 2-N.1 for weekly or bi-weekly checkoff on sixty days' notice, while 2-N.1 itself fixes deduction from the second pay check of each month and remittance within thirty days. Until the amendment is made, which schedule governs is unstated.

The letter promises only that The Times "is happy to continue our discussions and review" of the Union's pension proposals, creating no obligation to reach or implement anything. Against 17-D's statement that the parties have bargained and settled these subjects for the term, its status is unclear.

The Lancaster transport proposal is conditioned on "such transport did not involve the Times in increased costs," the same undefined qualifier used in 9-B, and the letter commits only to discussion "before the operation begins." Neither the cost test nor the outcome of the discussion is fixed.

The program is to be set up only "if a sufficient number of employees are interested," with no number stated and no one designated to decide sufficiency. "Another acceptable bank" is likewise unqualified as to whose acceptance is required.

This promises Bostrum seats and under-the-seat heaters only in "new trucks purchased for The News," while 3-H.1 requires that within thirty days of the effective date "all motor vehicles shall be equipped with heaters and defrosters" maintained in good working condition. The letter's narrower undertaking sits against the contract's general one.

The News undertakes to require no further payments once "the six payments referred to in the Memorandum have been made," whereas the Memorandum of Understanding provides for monthly $1,250 installments against a principal of $177,844. Six such payments would discharge a small fraction of the sum the Memorandum says the Union will pay.

The letter is printed out of order, with the stray line "Newspoint written agreements" preceding the body and the closing sentence broken off at "The News will abide by all." What the commitment covers beyond the 48-inch skid-height award cannot be read from the text.

A memorandum deleted from the prior agreement "shall be applicable" if "there be a problem in the future arising thereunder," reviving a document that the parties agreed to delete on a condition that is nowhere defined. What counts as such a problem, and who decides, is unstated.

The letter addresses "eligibility for the Medill Plan," a plan named nowhere else in the Agreement and apparently a mistranscription. The rules of eligibility are left to be posted unilaterally by the Benefit Department.

Deductions are for "a reasonable period of time designated by the employee" on an assignment "satisfactory to the Publisher," leaving both duration and form to undefined standards. Nothing says what makes an assignment satisfactory.

The acknowledgment that the Agreement "prohibits the subcontracting of bargaining unit deliveries except as it may exist pursuant to the contract" is circular and must be read against 3-E, 3-F and 2-E.2(d), which preserve combined delivery through wholesalers and expansion of work to over-the-road carriers. Which of those practices survives as permitted subcontracting is exactly what the letter leaves open.

The obligation to issue separate vacation checks arises only "when the planned DEC System is installed and operational," a condition with no date and wholly within The News' control. Whether the promise is enforceable before then is unaddressed.
The annual statement of pension-credited shifts is again conditioned on the DEC System being "installed and operational," with no deadline for that condition. The reporting duty may never mature.

The News undertakes to report "credited shifts for which contributions were not made," a category that presupposes shifts carrying pension credit without a contribution — something 13-I.1, which ties contributions to shifts worked up to five per week, does not define. What makes an uncontributed shift "credited" is unstated.
The thirty-day deadline for retroactive payments is excused "if delayed because of an emergency or Act of God," neither term being defined nor limited in duration. The excuse has no outer boundary.
The Company agreed only that it "would explore the purchase and use of dehumidifiers," an undertaking to consider rather than to act. No standard, timetable or outcome is fixed.

The promise is to provide "sixers" for Newspoint night men "in the same percentage as they are currently available" to the day shift, using an undefined trade term and an unfixed baseline date. The quantity owed cannot be determined.
